items.title: Building a Career in Web Development with AI-Powered Full Stack Skills
items.abstract: Web development is changing as businesses adopt new technologies to improve their digital services. Companies need websites, web applications, and software platforms that offer a smooth user experience, protect customer data, and support business growth. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is adding new capabilities to this process by helping developers write code, test applications, solve technical problems, and build intelligent features. Full-stack development gives professionals the skills to work on both the front end and the back end of an application. When combined with AI-powered development tools, these skills can help developers build useful digital products and adapt to changing industry requirements. For aspiring professionals, a career in web development involves more than learning a programming language. It requires an understanding of application design, databases, APIs, testing, deployment, and security. AI knowledge can extend these skills by helping developers automate routine tasks and integrate intelligent services into web applications. The Changing Role of Web Developers Web developers traditionally build and maintain websites and applications by writing code, connecting databases, testing features, and fixing errors. Modern development also requires collaboration with designers, product managers, security teams, and other engineers. AI tools are changing parts of this workflow. Developers can use them to generate code suggestions, explain unfamiliar functions, draft documentation, and create initial test cases. This may reduce time spent on some repetitive tasks. However, AI-generated code is not always correct or secure. Developers must understand the underlying logic and check the output before using it in a live application. They must also confirm that the code meets performance requirements and follows the project's standards. This change increases the value of problem-solving and technical judgement. Developers who understand programming fundamentals can evaluate AI suggestions more effectively than those who depend on generated code without understanding it. A career in web development can therefore benefit from a balanced skill set that combines coding knowledge, AI literacy, communication, and continuous learning. Research and Market Trends Shaping Career Opportunities Industry research provides useful evidence about the skills and technology roles expected to become more important. These trends support the case for learning full-stack development and AI, although they do not guarantee employment for individual candidates.Learners exploring a Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can use this growing intersection of software engineering and artificial intelligence as a starting point for developing industry-relevant skills. Global employment outlook The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies software and application developers among the fastest-growing job categories through 2030. It also lists AI and big data, networks and cybersecurity, and technological literacy among the skills expected to increase in importance. The report draws on more than 1,000 employers representing over 14 million workers across 55 economies. Its findings indicate that technology-related changes will affect both job requirements and workforce training. For aspiring web developers, this highlights the importance of learning core programming skills while remaining open to new tools and development methods. India's technology industry NASSCOM's Annual Strategic Review 2025 estimated that India's technology industry generated more than US$282.6 billion in revenue in FY2025, including hardware. It also projected that the industry could reach US$300 billion in FY2026. Engineering research and development, digital engineering, and global capability centres are among the areas contributing to India's technology ecosystem. These organisations support software development, product engineering, cloud services, and business transformation. This industry context creates a reason for learners to develop relevant technical skills. However, overall industry revenue is not the same as the number of available web development jobs. Actual hiring depends on employer requirements, business conditions, experience, and technical ability. Research on AI-assisted programming A controlled experiment published by researchers associated with Microsoft Research examined the effect of GitHub Copilot on a JavaScript programming task. Participants with access to the AI assistant completed the specified task 55.8% faster than participants in the control group. This result demonstrates the potential value of AI assistance in a defined setting. It does not mean that every software project will be completed at the same speed. Complex applications still require design, testing, security reviews, debugging, and coordination between team members. The practical lesson is to use AI tools to support development while retaining human responsibility for the final product. Core Skills for a Career in Full Stack Development A strong technical foundation helps developers build applications that work reliably. AI tools can support this process, but they cannot replace an understanding of how software systems operate. Front-end development Front-end development focuses on the interface users interact with. HTML provides structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds interactive features. Developers can also learn frameworks such as React to create reusable components and manage complex interfaces. Responsive design and accessibility are important because applications must work across different devices and meet the needs of different users. AI assistants can help create initial interface components, but developers must check the design, usability, browser compatibility, and performance. Back-end development Back-end development handles application logic, data processing, authentication, and communication between services. Common technologies include Node.js, Python, Java, and their related frameworks. Developers should understand how to create APIs, manage user permissions, validate inputs, and handle errors. These skills help them build applications that are reliable and secure. Databases and APIs Databases store information such as customer profiles, orders, transactions, and product records. Knowledge of SQL, database design, data validation, and access control helps developers manage this information. APIs connect different systems. A web application may use them to communicate with payment gateways, cloud platforms, analytics services, or AI models. Understanding these connections is essential when building complete applications. Cloud, DevOps, and security Web development does not end when the code is written. Applications must be deployed, monitored, updated, and protected against security threats. Developers can benefit from learning Git, automated testing, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD), containers, and cloud platforms. They should also understand secure authentication, data privacy, and the risks of exposing confidential information to unapproved AI tools. A Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can be considered by learners who want to study these technologies as part of a structured development path. Using AI Tools to Build Better Applications AI can support developers throughout the application lifecycle, from planning to maintenance. Its usefulness depends on the task, the quality of the input, and the developer's ability to evaluate the output. Code generation and debugging AI coding assistants can suggest functions, explain error messages, and create initial versions of repetitive code. Developers can use these suggestions to explore possible solutions and learn unfamiliar technologies. Before accepting generated code, they should review the logic, run tests, and check for security issues. This practice helps reduce the risk of introducing errors into an application. AI-powered application features Generative AI can help businesses add features such as chat assistants, document summaries, natural-language search, and personalised recommendations. For example, a customer support application could use an AI model to answer questions based on approved company documents. The full stack developer would build the user interface, manage access controls, connect APIs, and create the systems required to retrieve relevant information. Retrieval-augmented generation and AI agents Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects AI models with information retrieved from selected data sources. It can help applications produce responses based on relevant documents rather than relying only on information learned during model training. AI agents can use approved tools to complete defined multi-step tasks. These systems require clear permissions, monitoring, error handling, and human oversight when actions carry risk. Learning these concepts can help developers move beyond basic websites and explore more advanced applications. Career Paths and Professional Scope Full stack development can support several career paths, depending on a candidate's interests, technical knowledge, and experience. Full Stack Developer: Builds and maintains both front-end and back-end components. Front-End Developer: Creates interactive and accessible user interfaces. Back-End Developer: Develops server-side systems, APIs, and database connections. AI Application Developer: Integrates AI models and services into software products. Software Engineer: Designs, tests, and maintains software systems. Cloud or DevOps Engineer: Supports deployment, infrastructure, automation, and application monitoring. items.title: Building Resilient Telecom Operators through Artificial Intelligence: A CTE-Based Approach to Autonomous Network and Business Operations
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing where competitive advantage comes from in telecommunications. It used to depend mainly on network assets - spectrum, infrastructure, reach. Increasingly, it depends on how intelligent, adaptable, and resilient the systems running those assets are. This paper builds on the Comprehensive Techno-Economic (CTE) Model and its AI-augmented extension (AI-CTE) to propose a resilience framework that covers both autonomous network operations and autonomous business operations. Previous AI-CTE work formalized AI maturity, augmentation, dependency, and governance constructs, but mostly at the Technical Level. This paper extends that work in two directions. First, it introduces a Network Resilience Composite, combining the existing AI Resilience Score with a new Shock Absorption Capacity metric to quantify how well autonomous networks withstand and recover from disruptive events. Second, it develops three new AI-augmented equations at the Business Level - product and service resilience, customer and revenue resilience, and workforce resilience - which together make up a Business Resilience Index. These technical and business constructs, together with an Environmental/Governance Resilience Index, are combined into a single Telecom Operator Resilience Index (TORI). An illustrative application, extending a previously published case study, shows how the index can expose a gap between strong technical autonomy and weaker business-level resilience, giving operators concrete guidance on where to prioritize AI investment. The paper closes with an implementation roadmap and a discussion of limitations and future research directions. KeyWords: Comprehensive Techno-Economic Model, AI-CTE, Organizational Resilience, Autonomous Networks, Telecom Operators, AI Maturity Indeks.

items.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

items.title: Cognitive workload across subjective and electrodermal measures in relation to previous-night sleep
items.abstract: Introduction Cognitive workload is commonly assessed using both subjective and physiological indicators, although these measures may reflect different aspects of task-related strain. Sleep duration may further modify perceived task demand without producing proportional changes in physiological activation. This study examined the association between perceived cognitive workload and electrodermal task reactivity, and explored whether previous-night short sleep was associated with higher subjective workload without increased electrodermal activation. Methods A total of 52 adults were initially assessed; two were excluded due to violation of predefined eligibility criteria, resulting in a final analytical sample of 50 participants. Participants reported previous-night sleep duration and subjective sleep quality, completed a 5-min resting baseline, and then performed the Determination Test from the Vienna Test System. Electrodermal activity was recorded continuously during baseline and task performance, while perceived workload was assessed after the task using the NASA Task Load Index. Task-related electrodermal reactivity was calculated as GSR task–baseline difference, and participants were classified into short-sleep (< 7 h) and normal-sleep (≥7 h) groups. Results NASA-TLX total workload was not significantly associated with GSR task–baseline difference (rho = 0.126, p = 0.383). In the uncorrected threshold-based comparison, participants with short sleep reported higher perceived workload than those with normal sleep (64.44 ± 8.31 vs. 58.70 ± 9.57; p = 0.027), whereas GSR task–baseline difference was nearly identical between groups (4.57 ± 2.19 vs. 4.61 ± 2.93 μS; p = 0.884). However, the workload difference did not survive FDR correction across exploratory subgroup comparisons and should therefore be interpreted as a nominal finding. Discussion Overall, perceived workload and electrodermal reactivity showed limited correspondence, whereas the sleep-related analyses did not provide consistent evidence of an association with either outcome.

items.title: Communicating Uncertainty in AI-Supported Nurse Scheduling: Expert Co-Design and Evaluation of an Explainable AI Prototype
items.abstract: Nurse scheduling is a complex optimization problem in which nurses are assigned to shifts to meet staffing demands while complying with working-time limits, qualification requirements, and other operational and regulatory constraints. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to support this process by forecasting future staffing needs and providing advice on how to improve shift scheduling. Effective human-AI collaboration in nurse scheduling requires users to understand, interpret, and appropriately act on AI forecasts and advice. However, it remains insufficiently understood how healthcare professionals use transparency mechanisms like uncertainty communication and AI advice explanations when making staffing decisions. Applying a human-centered design approach, we iteratively developed a prototype decision support system for nurse scheduling and evaluated it through a mixed-methods user study with expert users. Using thematic analysis, questionnaire data, and eye tracking, we examine how healthcare professionals interact with the system and how uncertainty communication and explanations of AI advice influence understanding, decision confidence, trust, and usability. We found that the uncertainty communicated in AI forecasts was frequently misinterpreted and reduced decision confidence. Explanations were generally perceived positively, but did not significantly affect decision confidence or advice acceptance. We conclude with eight design implications derived from our findings, providing insights for the design of more transparent and effective AI-supported decision support tools in healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
items.abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.abstract: Forecasting and optimization form an integrated foundation for the intelligent management of complex systems in industry, logistics, energy, transportation, and service operations. The interaction of multiple components, changing operating conditions, and interconnected decisions creates valuable opportunities for data-driven modeling and adaptive resource allocation. This study presents a comparative literature-based analysis of statistical forecasting, machine learning, deep learning, mathematical optimization, and reinforcement learning approaches. Their suitability is examined in relation to temporal patterns, explanatory variables, uncertainty representation, computational requirements, and decision objectives. Particular attention is given to hybrid architectures that connect probabilistic forecasts with optimization models and continuously updated decisions. The synthesis establishes a conceptual framework for evaluating forecasting quality alongside operational performance and identifies promising directions for intelligent management of dynamic complex systems.

items.title: Consumer Decision-Making in Digital Commerce: Effects of Virtual Influencer Motive Attributions on Trust, Perceived Risk, and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: In AI-enabled digital commerce, consumers evaluate virtual influencers (VIs) not only through source characteristics but also by inferring why they create content and recommend products. This study examines how perceived intrinsic and commercially oriented extrinsic motives are associated with trust, perceived risk, and purchase intention. Survey data from 295 South Korean consumers aged 20–39 were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 23.0 for descriptive and reliability analyses and IBM SPSS Amos 24.0 for confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Perceived intrinsic motivation was positively associated with trust but was not significantly associated with perceived risk or directly with purchase intention. Perceived extrinsic motivation was negatively associated with trust and purchase intention and positively associated with perceived risk. Trust was positively associated with purchase intention, whereas the conditional association of perceived risk was nonsignificant. Supplementary bootstrap analyses supported specific indirect associations through trust for both motive attributions, consistent with full (indirect-only) mediation for intrinsic motivation and partial mediation for extrinsic motivation within the specified model. Neither specific indirect association through perceived risk was significant. These findings distinguish consumers’ confidence in a recommending persona from their uncertainty about a recommended purchase and identify trust as a central statistical mediator of motive attribution and purchase intention in VI marketing.

items.title: Deepfakes and bots in digital disinformation driven by malicious artificial intelligence
items.abstract: In an increasingly uncertain digital environment, how do we know if what we see is real? Deepfakes, which include videos with fake faces, synthetic audio, and manipulated documents, along with social bots that interact and persuade as if they were humans, represent a growing threat driven by malicious artificial intelligence. These technologies not only spread disinformation but also generate collective emotions such as fear, indignation, and distrust, affecting democratic stability and social cohesion. Faced with this reality, this article develops a bibliometric study and a scoping review of the literature (2014-2024) based on 316 documents indexed in Scopus, with the purpose of identifying trends, influential authors, methodological approaches, and research gaps on the use of artificial intelligence in disinformation. The results show an annual growth of 97%, an average age of 2.2 years per document, 19.7 average citations, and an h-index of 37, evidencing the sustained expansion and scientific interest in the detection of deepfakes and bots as central challenges of the digital ecosystem. Production is concentrated in India, the United States, and China. The co-occurrence analysis confirms the main research axes in deepfake detection, deep learning, and CNNs, along with the growing prominence of synthetic speech, diffusion models, and the economic and social effects of social media. Future research should address the role of AI in political communication, in particular its links to disinformation, polarization, and emotional influence, as well as the impact of the EU AI Act, the need for standardised metrics, and the emergence of transnational frameworks for digital governance.

items.abstract: The encyclical Magnifica Humanitas of H. H. León XIV reflects on the challenges that artificial intelligence poses to human dignity, emphasizing that technological progress acquires meaning only when it serves the human person and the common good. The document warns about the risks of the technocratic paradigm, the dehumanization of relationships, information manipulation, educational inequalities, and the impact of automation on work. It also proposes a culture of love, solidarity, and justice as the foundation for guiding scientific and technological development. From the perspective of Christian humanism, it highlights the need for an integral education that fosters critical thinking, ethical discernment, and the responsible use of new technologies. Finally, it argues that artificial intelligence should complement, rather than replace, moral responsibility, freedom, and the transcendent vocation of the human person, thereby promoting an authentically human and inclusive form of development.

items.title: Design Implications for Teacher-Configurable Generative AI Writing Tools: A Participatory Design Study with StoryBot
items.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) tools become accessible, their integration into K–12 writing presents opportunities and challenges. This study partnered with 21 primary school teachers in a participatory co-design process to develop StoryBot, a teacher-configurable GenAI story-authoring platform. Teachers identified instructional needs and learning outcomes that informed system features, including genre-specific writing scaffolds, configurable prompts, and constraints on full-text generation to preserve student voice. The platform positions educators as co-designers of AI behavior rather than passive users. We conducted a pilot writing workshop with 13 youth (ages 8–12) and a focus group with six educators to examine how the platform influenced students’ writing behaviors and classroom integration. Findings demonstrate the value of teacher co-design and configurable AI systems in aligning GenAI tools with pedagogical priorities and practices. We present design implications for teacher-configurable GenAI writing systems that support student agency, ethical safeguards, and instructional alignment in human–AI coauthoring environments.

items.title: DEVELOPING SOCIOLINGUISTIC THINKING IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PEDAGOGICAL PERSPECTIVES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a new participant in everyday and educational communication. Learners now talk to chatbots, use machine translation and receive automated feedback on their writing. This conceptual paper examines how these tools affect the development of sociolinguistic thinking, understood as the ability to select, interpret and adapt language forms according to social context, participants and communicative goals. Drawing on sociocultural theory, social learning theory, sociolinguistics and intercultural pedagogy, the paper outlines the cognitive, social and emotional mechanisms involved and analyzes the opportunities and risks of AI as a language model and interlocutor. It then proposes five pedagogical conditions for developing sociolinguistic thinking in AI-supported learning environments: critical AI literacy, contextualized task design, teacher mediation, comparison of human and machine language, and a supportive psychological climate.

items.title: DIGITAL CONSUMER BEHAVIOR: BAGAIMANA TEKNOLOGI, ALGORITMA, DAN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MENGUBAH CARA MANUSIA BERPIKIR, MERASA, DAN MENGAMBIL KEPUTUSAN
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies, including the internet, social media, e-commerce platforms, online marketplaces, and artificial intelligence-based applications, has fundamentally transformed consumer behavior in the digital marketplace. Consumers are no longer passive recipients of marketing messages; instead, they actively seek information, evaluate alternatives, engage with brands, and make purchasing decisions through various digital channels. This transformation has led to the emergence of Digital Consumer Behavior as a critical determinant of marketing effectiveness and business sustainability in the digital economy. This study aims to examine the influence of Digital Consumer Behavior on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision, as well as to investigate the mediating role of Consumer Trust in this relationship. A quantitative research approach was employed using a survey method involving 100 active digital platform users who had conducted online purchases within the previous six months. Respondents were selected through purposive sampling, and data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The empirical findings reveal that Digital Consumer Behavior has a positive and significant effect on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision. Furthermore, Consumer Trust significantly influences Purchase Decision. The mediation analysis demonstrates that Consumer Trust significantly mediates the relationship between Digital Consumer Behavior and Purchase Decision. The coefficient of determination indicates that the model explains of the variance in Consumer Trust of the variance in Purchase Decision having a strong relationship. These findings provide theoretical support for the integration of digital consumer behavior and consumer trust perspectives within contemporary marketing literature. From a managerial perspective, businesses should focus on delivering informative, interactive, and trustworthy digital experiences to strengthen consumer trust and enhance purchasing decisions. The study concludes that technological advancements have significantly reshaped how consumers acquire information, build trust, evaluate product alternatives, and make purchasing decisions in a faster, more efficient, and increasingly rational manner.

items.title: Digital Wisdom and GenAI
items.abstract: Within the framework of the European Erasmus+ STIAEM project, the authors of this study deconstruct the assumed homogeneity of “digital natives” regarding generative artificial intelligence adoption. Utilizing a sample of 2,052 secondary school students, the research architecture applies confirmatory factor analysis, extended Bayesian information criterion graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator network analysis, and latent profile analysis. Results identify distinct student profiles based on engagement and familiarity, revealing a profound relational decoupling between technological motivation and situated ethical choices. Under academic deadline pressures, nearly all (92.74%) of the sample participants succumbed to automation bias, uncritically accepting machine hallucinations. This behavioral paradox demonstrates that superficial digital fluency masks severe deficits in epistemic validation and independent thought. Consequently, in this paper the authors argue for shifting from product to process evaluation and integrating explicit algor-ethics interventions within school curricula to develop reflexive, human-centric algorithmic citizenship.

items.title: Discernment in generative AI assisted instructional design: An evaluation map and design heuristics for learning experience designers
items.abstract: Existing research shows that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increases instructional design efficiency. However, there are concerns about pedagogical quality, accuracy and content bias. While prior studies address student passivity in evaluating AI content, the potential for designers to be passive in creating instructional materials remains largely unexplored. This article addresses design safeguards for AI-assisted course and learning-material development through two complementary tools: the Discernment Map, an evaluation checkpoint for instructional designers, and a set of design heuristics. The study is conceptual and design-oriented: both tools were drafted from the literature on AI fluency, automation bias and schema theory, and then refined through structured consultations with six experienced instructional designers in higher education. Though yet to be empirically validated, the practice-informed tools work at two levels: the Map operationalises human oversight of AI outputs across Product, Process and Performance dimensions for each AI-generated artefact, while the heuristics extend discernment into the design of the learning experience itself, so that learners must evaluate rather than accept AI outputs. Both are agile micro-governance tools that integrate critical judgment directly into design workflows. The approach is intended to protect long-term instructional quality against the collective erosion that unchecked AI adoption risks, and to support intentional engagement with AI that reduces automation bias.

items.title: Dynamic engagement patterns during collaborative reasoning discussions and their relations to adolescents’ individual reasoning
items.abstract: Background Collaborative Reasoning (CR) is a dialogic, learner-centered instructional approach shown to promote learners’ higher-order thinking. However, existing research has paid less attention to how learners engage in CR processes and how the temporal dynamics of engagement relate to the development of individual reasoning. Aims To address this gap, this study investigated the temporal development of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement during CR discussions and examined how evolving engagement patterns were associated with subsequent individual reasoning. Sample The participants were 29 seventh-graders from a middle school in China. The students formed four discussion groups, and each group participated in seven CR discussions. Methods The 28 discussions were video-coded for cognitive, emotional, and behavioral interactions (6868 codes). Process mining and epistemic network analysis were used to model shifts in engagement patterns. Individual reasoning was assessed through post-discussion essays. Results Engagement patterns shifted dynamically over time, moving from socially shared regulation to sustained knowledge co-construction. Groups differed in the timing and trajectory of this transition: some groups shifted earlier, whereas others engaged in prolonged regulatory exchanges. The group characterized by later transitions produced fewer basic argumentative elements but more advanced elements in their individual essays. Conclusions This study highlights dynamic engagement patterns as an important link between collaborative processes and learning outcomes and underscores the importance of understanding temporal configurations of regulation and knowledge co-construction in collaborative learning.

items.title: Educational Recommender Systems for Metacognitive and Self-Regulated Learning Support: An Algorithmic Systematic Review
items.abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.

items.title: Empathetic responses by AI legal assistants and user over-disclosure: evidence from an online survey experiment
items.abstract: Introduction Generative AI legal assistants rely on users to describe events, evidence, and transaction histories, yet the same accounts may contain private information that is unnecessary for legal guidance. Empathetic language may affect how selectively users decide what to provide. Methods A one-factor between-subjects online survey experiment on Wenjuanxing randomly assigned 360 participants to rational, mildly empathetic, or highly empathetic AI legal responses (n = 120 per condition). Participants completed 1-5 Likert-type measures of parasocial response, privacy boundary judgment, and over-disclosure intention, together with related relational measures, and then answered an open-ended disclosure task. Results The empathy manipulation was successful, F (2,357) = 524.170, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.746. Stronger empathetic responses increased parasocial response (η 2 = 0.428), reduced privacy boundary judgment (η 2 = 0.242), and increased over-disclosure intention (η 2 = 0.406). The coded non-essential disclosure score rose from 0.994 in the rational condition to 6.132 in the highly empathetic condition, F (2,357) = 170.795, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.489. Necessary case facts remained stable, F (2,357) = 0.245, p = 0.783. Bootstrap analysis yielded an indirect effect through parasocial response of 0.214, 95% CI [0.151, 0.283], and a sequential indirect effect through parasocial response and privacy boundary judgment of 0.063, 95% CI [0.033, 0.098]. Discussion Within this consumer-dispute scenario, stronger empathetic cues reduced users' selectivity about which information was appropriate to provide. Data-minimization prompts and evidence-oriented questioning may help retain limited emotional support without encouraging unnecessary disclosure.

items.abstract: This thesis analyzes the didactic potential of using interactive and innovative pedagogical technologies to enhance students’ learning activity, cognitive engagement, educational motivation, and participation in collaborative activities within differentiated instruction. Particular attention is paid to adapting interactive methods to differences in students’ levels of knowledge, interests, pace of learning, and individual educational needs. The role of problem-based learning, project-based learning, gamification, cooperative learning, the flipped classroom model, multimedia tools, and other innovative approaches in differentiated instruction is examined.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is one of the major technological advancements of this century, bearing incredible potential for users through AI-powered applications and tools in numerous domains. Being often black-box (i.e., its decision-making process is unintelligible), developers typically resort to eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to interpret the behavior of AI models to produce systems that are transparent, fair, reliable, and trustworthy. However, presenting explanations to the user is not trivial and is often left as a secondary aspect of the system’s design process, leading to AI systems that are not useful to end-users. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review on Explanation User Interfaces (XUIs) to gain a deeper understanding of the solutions and design guidelines employed in the academic literature to effectively present explanations to users. items.title: Exploration or exploitation? The double-edged effects of AI use modes on radical creativity: evidence from AI-enabled drug discovery
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted in corporate innovation activities, yet prior research has not reached a consensus on whether it is more conducive to incremental or radical innovation. For radical innovation, which depends on highly novel ideas, realizing the value of AI depends not only on whether AI is adopted but, more importantly, on whether employees can use it creatively to transcend established knowledge boundaries. Drawing on environmental dynamism and the exploration–exploitation perspective, this study develops a theoretical model linking leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism, employees’ AI use modes, leader temporal myopia, and employee radical creativity in the context of AI-enabled drug discovery. We distinguish leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism into perceived technological dynamism and perceived market dynamism, and employees’ AI use into exploratory and exploitative AI use. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and three-wave matched survey data from 368 leader–employee dyads. The results show that leader-perceived technological dynamism is positively associated with employee exploratory AI use, whereas leader-perceived market dynamism is positively associated with employee exploitative AI use. Exploratory AI use is positively associated with employee radical creativity, whereas exploitative AI use is negatively associated with it. Leader temporal myopia weakens the positive conditional indirect relationship of technological dynamism with radical creativity through exploratory AI use and strengthens the negative conditional indirect relationship of market dynamism with radical creativity through exploitative AI use. By adopting a knowledge-activity perspective, this study reveals the differentiated relationships between AI use modes and radical creativity and further explains how perceptions of the external environment, leaders’ temporal orientation, and employees’ AI use behaviors are differentially related. The findings provide a theoretical basis and practical implications for helping firms engaged in AI-enabled drug discovery guide employees toward effective AI use and enhance radical creativity.

items.title: Fostering team learning for educational innovation: An academic development initiative on genAI and assessment
items.abstract: Abstract Drawing on the notion of workplace learning this study examines how academic development can design and facilitate team learning in the academic workplace to support co-constructive educational innovation. Based on a qualitative case study at a Swiss University of Teacher Education, it analyses a participatory initiative addressing generative artificial intelligence (genAI) in assessment. The staged process combined SWOT-based collective sense-making, a design sprint, selective project funding, and facilitated reflection during project development. Data consisted of process documentation and collaboratively generated written reflections, which were analysed and refined through iterative feedback and co-writing. The findings show how structured formats, shared artefacts, and deliberate facilitation enabled participants to make distributed expertise visible, develop shared problem understandings, form project teams, and move from exchange towards co-construction and coordinated experimentation. At the same time, public pitching, funding decisions, time pressures, and institutional constraints created tensions between collaboration and competition, openness and focus, and participation and decision-making. The study suggests that academic development can support educational innovation by acting as facilitator, trust-building broker, and co-learner. Its contribution lies in conceptualising participatory innovation processes as workplace-learning arrangements that connect emerging team-learning processes with local experimentation and wider institutional conversations, while recognising that organisational learning requires further institutional uptake.

items.title: From Circuits to Policies: A Review and Taxonomy of Decision Making and Strategy Selection in LLMs and LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language models and the agents built on them can reach the same outcome through different internal computations, reasoning trajectories, and system-level policies. Existing reviews typically treat mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, agent architectures, and safety separately, leaving no common framework for analyzing how a system represents alternatives, evaluates them, commits to one, executes it, and revises that choice. This article presents a structured review and a faceted taxonomy of decision making and strategy selection in LLMs and LLM-based agents. The framework separates system locus—model, harness, or their tested interaction—from temporal scope—a single forward pass or call, a reasoning episode, or an agent trajectory—and decomposes decision making into six functional stages from state representation to update or termination. Five claim-specific evidential relations distinguish behavioral observation, representation decoding, causal influence, controlled manipulation, and mechanistic explanation, while robustness is assessed separately across prompts, tasks, models, harness configurations, and independent replication. Across the literature, evidence is strongest for local mechanisms within individual model calls and substantially weaker for persistent strategies across agent trajectories. The central unresolved gap is cross-scope continuity: few studies follow the same decision variable from internal representation through commitment, executed action, and subsequent feedback. A July 2026 agent-security incident is used to illustrate how the framework converts observed coordination and constraint circumvention into testable causal hypotheses.

items.title: From tool to Coauthor
items.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence into contemporary artistic practices requires reconsidering creativity, authorship, and originality, transforming relationships between artist, tool, and artwork. Unlike conventional digital technologies, which execute operations defined by creators, generative systems exhibit operational autonomy, producing partly unpredictable visual configurations. This raises questions about algorithmic intervention and the possibility of attributing co-authorship to artificial intelligence systems. This article examines the relationship between human creators and generative technologies through computational creativity, distributed authorship, and philosophical perspectives on nonhuman agency. It distinguishes systems’ operational autonomy from artists’ intentional autonomy, arguing that algorithmic participation does not necessarily imply creative subjectivity comparable to human experience. It also examines the aesthetic and conceptual implications of human–machine collaboration and the reorganisation of artistic practices through generation, selection, interpretation, and post-production. The study argues that generative artificial intelligence reconfigures human authorship, shifting creative activity from direct execution toward intention formulation, system configuration, and critical evaluation. Artists therefore retain a decisive role in directing the process and taking responsibility for its artistic outcomes. Algorithmic co-authorship serves as a conceptual tool for understanding these emerging production relationships, without implying legal authorship or artificial consciousness.

items.title: Generative AI -Based Employee Skill Gap Analysis and Personalized Upskilling Recommendations
items.abstract: Rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into enterprise processes highlights critical gaps in workforce readiness in terms of skills required for successful implementation of new technologies. This paper introduces a framework which will enable use of generative AI for conducting dynamic skill gap analysis and providing personalized recommendations for upskilling. The framework includes mapping of competencies according to shifting role demands, individual performance assessment through AI and adaptation of learning path for each individual based on results. Using the information obtained from surveys about AI adoption in enterprises and competency maps developed in recent research, this paper will show how generative AI can be used for making static learning programs adaptive and relevant to the current needs of learners. The problem discussed in the paper is related to not only technical AI literacy, but also to human skills, such as critical thinking, ethical decision-making and change management. Comparative analysis of methods shows that personalized training offered by generative AI is more engaging and relevant than generic models of training programs.

items.title: Generative AI in Distance Education: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Personalization, Inclusion and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new possibilities for distance education through conversational learning support, personalised explanations, automated feedback and multilingual assistance. However, its integration also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, unequal access, information reliability, learner autonomy and data privacy. This paper develops a conceptual framework for integrating GenAI into distance education through a human-in-the-loop approach. Drawing on relevant scholarly literature and international educational policy documents, the study examines the relationship between AI-supported personalisation, inclusive learning, human oversight and academic accountability. It proposes an integrated framework in which teachers and learners retain meaningful decision-making authority while AI provides supplementary educational support. The framework comprises five dimensions: human agency, equitable access, learner-centred personalisation, academic integrity and responsible data governance. The paper argues that technological availability alone cannot guarantee educational improvement; effective implementation also requires AI literacy, appropriate assessment practices, institutional policies and continuous human evaluation. The proposed framework offers conceptual guidance for higher-education institutions seeking to adopt GenAI responsibly in distance-learning environments. As a conceptual contribution, it requires subsequent empirical evaluation to establish its applicability across different educational contexts.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI MARKETING AND PURCHASE INTENTION AMONG GENERATION Z: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF BRAND PERCEPTION
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping digital marketing by enabling personalised, scalable, and innovative content, while simultaneously raising concerns regarding authenticity and consumer trust. This study examines how Perceived Authenticity, Perceived Personalization, and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation influence Brand Perception and Purchase Intention among Generation Z consumers, with Brand Perception serving as a mediating mechanism. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using data from 425 Generation Z consumers collected through a structured questionnaire based on five-point Likert-type scales. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson and Spearman correlations, multiple regression, variance inflation factors, HC3 robust standard errors, and bootstrapped mediation analysis based on 5,000 resamples. The findings indicate that Perceived Authenticity (β = .234), Perceived Personalization (β = .160), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .407) significantly and positively influence Brand Perception. Brand Perception significantly predicts Purchase Intention (β = .520). Significant indirect effects were observed for Perceived Authenticity (β = .122), Perceived Personalization (β = .083), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .212) through Brand Perception. The findings demonstrate that consumer responses to GenAI marketing translate into purchase intention substantially through broader brand evaluations. The study highlights the importance of combining AI-enabled innovation and personalization with authenticity and consistent brand positioning.

items.title: Generative AI Use and Learning Productivity Among Google Gemini Users in Bangladesh: An Integrated TAM-Self-Regulated Learning Model
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p < .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p < .001) and PU (β = .218, p < .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p < .001) and SRL (β = .202, p < .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

items.title: Generative AI Use and the Student Well-Being Paradox in Higher Education: Efficiency-Gain Retention, Performance Escalation, and Relative Competition
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce the time and cognitive effort required for university learning, yet technical efficiency does not necessarily translate into improved student well-being. This article develops and tests a conversion account of this paradox by distinguishing efficiency gains that remain available as student-controlled resources from gains that are associated with perceived increases in performance expectations, competitive pressure, verification work, and dependence. A sequential three-study mixed-methods program was conducted with undergraduates in Jiangxi Province. Study 1 used codebook thematic analysis of 42 interviews to identify six mechanisms linking immediate efficiency to resource retention or perceived pressure. Study 2 surveyed 1268 students across eight universities. GenAI use was strongly associated with perceived efficiency gains, but also with perceived performance-standard escalation and verification burden. Positive retention and negative competition pathways were similar in magnitude, yielding a nonsignificant total association with well-being; working-time retention strengthened the efficiency–well-being association. Because Study 2 was cross-sectional, these pathways are interpreted as indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Study 3 used a 2 × 2 experiment (N = 320) and found that AI access improved task quality and reduced completion time under both performance-norm conditions, whereas gains in autonomy, retained time, and state well-being were evident under the stable norm but not statistically distinguishable from zero under the escalated norm. The findings distinguish technical affordance from context-dependent conversion and suggest that responsible AI integration should consider whether efficiency gains remain available for learning, recovery, and student-directed use alongside productivity.

items.title: Generative AI-Guided Versus Human-Guided Learning from Errors in Higher Education: A Comparison of Student Perceptions
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support programming education, but its use in learning-from-errors activities has received limited research attention. This quasi-experimental study compared AI-guided and human-guided support in a structured learning-from-errors programming activity, focusing on students’ perceptions and their variability. A total of 59 college students completed the JavaScript error-detection and correction activity under AI-guided or human-guided support. Following the activity, students completed a questionnaire measuring perceived learning experience, satisfaction, general motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL), and self-efficacy. Between-group differences were examined using Mann–Whitney U tests, and differences in variability were examined using Levene’s tests. Students in the AI-guided condition reported significantly more positive learning experiences and greater satisfaction than those in the human-guided condition. They also reported significantly higher overall SRL and greater use of SRL strategies. No significant differences were found in general motivation, SRL motivation, SRL planning and organization, or self-efficacy. The AI-guided group showed significantly lower raw variability in satisfaction and self-efficacy. However, a sensitivity analysis did not establish that these variance differences remained after accounting for mean-related constraints on the bounded response scale. The findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a scaffold for error analysis when integrated in ways that maintain students’ active cognitive engagement.

items.abstract: This project documents the methods and analytical framework of a scoping review examining how generative artificial intelligence is used to support learning and research competency development among postgraduate nursing students. The review focuses on six competency domains: information literacy and evidence retrieval, evidence-based practice competency, research methodology and analytical skills, academic writing and scientific communication, critical thinking and research thinking, and AI literacy and responsible AI use. items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence: Ethical Considerations and Its Impact on Students’ Cognitive Skills
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, influencing how students learn, produce knowledge, and engage in assessments. This study examines the ethical implications of AI integration in university courses and its perceived impact on students’ cognitive skills. Using a mixed-methods secondary data analysis, survey data from 23,218 students across 109 countries and 252 teachers from China, Romania, India, and Brunei were analyzed to explore perceptions of AI capabilities, ethical boundaries, behavioral intentions, and cognitive outcomes. The results have shown that although students are aware of the potential of AI in improving the efficiency and content creation and assistance in the learning process, there are still concerns about overdependence, plagiarism, and lack of critical thinking. The views of faculty underline moral direction and the necessity of systematic assimilation. Developing upon these insights, a theoretical framework is developed that connects antecedent variables, behavior intentions and institutional context to two outcomes the cognitive impact and institutional influence. This framework offers a guide on how universities should introduce generative AI in a responsible manner, and strike a balance between ethical principles and training higher-order cognitive abilities.

items.title: Government Support, AI Adoption, and SME Innovation Performance: An Institutional Theory Perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to innovation in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet resource constraints limit their ability to exploit it. Governments worldwide provide institutional support to encourage SME AI adoption, but whether such support translates into innovation depends on internal organizational conditions that remain poorly understood. Drawing on institutional theory, this study treats government support as a source of coercive, normative, and mimetic pressure and develops an integrative conceptual model in which it influences SME innovation performance through AI adoption intensity, with organizational learning capability as a mediator and organizational readiness as a moderator. The model specifies that government support raises adoption intensity, which in turn enhances innovation performance; that organizational learning capability partially mediates this effect; and that organizational readiness strengthens the link between government support and adoption intensity. A quantitative, cross-sectional design is proposed: structured questionnaires will collect no fewer than 200 valid responses from SMEs, analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Theoretically, the study is expected to extend institutional theory from the adoption/non-adoption dichotomy to a continuous adoption-intensity construct and to position organizational learning as the channel transmitting adoption into innovation. Practically, it can inform the design of differentiated government policy and SME capability building.

items.title: Graph-Based Orchestration of Heterogeneous AI Models: A Control Node Approach to Composite Intelligence
items.abstract: We present a graph-based framework for Composite AI systems that integrate multiple AI techniques to address complex problems. We describe an architecture using specialized control nodes to orchestrate diverse models including planning, machine learning, constraint programming, and large language models. The system employs directed acyclic graphs and behavior trees to manage model relationships and execution sequencing. Our methodology encompasses data connectors, computational services, and a containerized deployment framework supporting hierarchical, sequential, and concurrent model composition patterns. Through case studies, we demonstrate how this architecture enables the creation of composite systems that leverage the strengths of multiple AI techniques within a unified operational schema, overcoming the limitations of single-model approaches.

items.title: GREEN TECH PARADOX An Analysis of AI in Environment Sustainability
items.abstract: Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into environmental sustainability strategies presents a critical dilemma known as the "Green Tech Paradox." While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to optimize resource allocation, predict climate patterns, and enhance energy efficiency across industrial sectors, its deployment carries substantial, often overlooked, ecological costs. This research provides a critical analysis of the dual role AI plays as both a catalyst for eco-innovations and a significant contributor to environmental degradation. On the positive frontier, AI-driven applications accelerate sustainability by enabling smart power grids, improving carbon capture systems, facilitating precision agriculture, and modeling complex environmental crises. Machine learning algorithms enhance operational efficiency, reducing waste and carbon footprints in manufacturing and logistics. However, these beneficial outcomes are counterbalanced by the escalating physical footprint of AI infrastructure. The training and continuous execution of complex neural networks demand massive amounts of electricity, heavily relying on fossil-fuel-dominant energy grids. Furthermore, data centers consume millions of liters of freshwater daily for cooling mechanisms, accelerating localized water scarcity, while the rapid obsolescence of specialized hardware generates growing volumes of hazardous electronic waste. This paper evaluates this structural tension through a multidimensional synthesis of secondary data, life-cycle assessments, and resource consumption metrics across global data centers. The analysis reveals that without stringent regulatory frameworks and sustainable design interventions, the environmental degradation caused by AI's hardware lifecycle risks surpassing its ecological benefits. Ultimately, the study advocates for a paradigm shift toward "Green AI"—prioritizing algorithmic efficiency, renewable energy integration for computing infrastructure, sustainable hardware lifecycle management, and policy-driven eco-design standards. By establishing transparent auditing protocols, researchers and industry leaders can mitigate the hidden ecological liabilities of artificial intelligence, ensuring that modern technological advancement aligns genuinely with global net-zero targets and long-term planetary boundaries. Keywords: Green AI, Climate change mitigation, Sustainable development goals (SDGs), Environmental governance, Lifecycle assessment of AI.

items.title: Green Transformational Leadership, Work Motivation, and Sustainable Employee Performance: The Role of Employee Engagement
items.abstract: Objectives: This study comprehensively investigates the underlying mechanisms through which green transformational leadership and work motivation influence sustainable employee performance. Specifically, the research evaluates the pivotal mediating role of employee engagement within the highly analytical and bureaucratic environment of Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank. Methodology: We employed an explanatory quantitative research design utilizing a cross-sectional survey approach. The empirical data were collected from a carefully determined sample of 158 permanent employees across four strategic departments at Bank Indonesia using a stratified random sampling approach. To test the complex structural relationships and mediation effects, we applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) using the SmartPLS 4 software, executing a rigorous bootstrapping procedure with 5,000 subsamples. Finding: The empirical analysis reveals a compelling theoretical anomaly where green transformational leadership does not directly drive sustainable employee performance. Conversely, intrinsic work motivation exerts a strong, positive, and direct impact on the sustainability of employee performance. More importantly, both green leadership and work motivation are highly effective in cultivating deep employee engagement. Consequently, employee engagement emerges as a significant driver of sustainable performance, acting as a full mediator for green transformational leadership and a partial mediator for work motivation. Conclusion: Employee engagement functions as an absolute psychological bridge in a central banking context. Without this deep emotional and cognitive involvement, top-down environmental leadership visions and latent intrinsic motivation cannot effectively materialize into resilient, long-term sustainable performance.

items.title: HelpMeOut: A Neuropsychology-Grounded Benchmark for Error-Aware Monitoring of Household Task Execution
items.abstract: We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.

items.title: Hierarchical DEMATEL-based key risk identification for urban public safety within grid management
items.abstract: With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models.

items.title: HIPA: A Human Information Processing Architecture for LLM Responses in Ergonomic Design
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for UI/UX evaluation and design decision support; however, their responses are often generated as implicit and unstructured outputs, making cognitive processes and judgment rationale difficult to trace. Moreover, the quality of LLM-based judgments may vary depending on users’ prompting proficiency, limiting the consistency of AI-assisted evaluation. This study proposes HIPA (Human Information Processing Architecture), a cognitive response architecture that structures LLM outputs based on the human information processing (HIP) model and investigates the manifestation of human cognitive stages in conventional LLM responses. HIPA maps four HIP stages—perception, working memory, decision making, and response execution—into a two-stage response structure consisting of information provision and judgment support through knowledge-grounded prompting with GPT-4o. An exploratory evaluation was conducted with seven participants with different prompting proficiency levels who assessed the same mobile login interface using a general LLM. Responses were coded according to HIP-stage manifestation using a three-point scale. The results showed that perception and response execution were consistently observed, whereas working memory and decision-making stages varied depending on prompt systematicity. These findings indicate that general LLM responses do not inherently provide cognitively structured judgment support. HIPA provides a human-centered framework for developing AI-assisted UI/UX evaluation systems based on human cognitive principles.

items.title: Historical development, current landscape and emerging trends of academic journals in human factors and ergonomics: Using a bibliometric analysis and a knowledge-domain mapping analysis
items.abstract: Human factors and ergonomics (HFE) is vital for optimising human-centred system design. This study aimed to synthesise research on HFE and examine its historical evolution, current landscape and emerging trends. A bibliometric analysis and a knowledge-domain mapping analysis were conducted to combine perspectives on journal development and article output. This study focused on 24 journals classified in the ergonomics category in the Journal Citation Reports of 2024. Critical information for the 24 HFE journals was investigated, including commencement year of publication, composition of editorial boards, number of published papers, publishing models, 2024 quartile rankings and impact factors and 5-year impact factors. Two visualisation tools, VOSviewer and CiteSpace, were used to perform the bibliometric analysis of the 26,026 HFE documents in the Web of Science Core Collection, spanning 2010 to 2024. Results showed that HFE literature has evolved from classical industrial origins to modern technological paradigms. Increased collaborations across different research areas to address HFE problems were observed. The review also identified key domain expansions across high-impact emerging HFE frontiers, including artificial intelligence, extended reality, autonomous vehicles and wearable technologies. Building upon these findings, the study may provide in-depth insights into the critical future HFE research directions.

items.title: How is automation related to work characteristics and employee well-being? A work design perspective
items.abstract: BackgroundAutomation, including both robots and AI, are increasingly implemented in the public sector to handle an increased demand for services while facing a shortage of staff. However, little is known of how automation is related to employees' work characteristics and well-being.ObjectiveThe purpose of the present study was to examine how automation is related to work characteristics and well-being in a national sample of social workers.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted with a sample of 1428 social workers in Sweden, comparing those working with automation technologies (e.g., robotization in terms of automated decision-making support in financial aid) to those without.ResultsThe findings indicate that automation is negatively related to relational aspects of work, such as beneficiary contact and social support, and increases perceived workload and role conflict. However, no significant differences were found on decision-making autonomy, role clarity, or skill variety. Despite these work design changes, no significant differences in well-being outcomes, such as burnout and vigor, were observed between the two groups.ConclusionThe findings suggest that automation may alter the nature of social work without necessarily changing employee well-being. These insights have implications for organizations seeking to implement automation in a way that supports employees' work experience and well-being.

items.title: HUMAN CAPITAL ASSESSMENT WITH AN APPROACH BASED ON INTEGRATING HETEROGENEOUS DATA AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE DIGITAL ECONOMY
items.abstract: The purpose of the research -This article examines human capital assessment through the integration of heterogeneous data and artificial intelligence in the context of the digital economy.The study aims to identify the interrelationships among artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and human capital, and to empirically evaluate how these factors influence productivity. Research methodology -The research applies analysis, comparison, systematization, grouping, and generalization methods.Its empirical part is based on panel data covering the period 2010-2024 and obtained from open international statistical databases.The analytical framework includes descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, unit root tests, cointegration analysis, multivariate regression modeling, and Granger causality testing.This methodological approach allows a comprehensive assessment of the interaction between artificial intelligence, digital transformation, human capital, and productivity.Results of the research -The findings show that artificial intelligence has a significant positive impact on productivity, while human capital strongly reinforces this effect.Digital transformation also contributes positively through better data processing and resource allocation.The results confirm long-run relationships among the variables and identify artificial intelligence and human capital as major drivers of productivity growth.Originality and scientific novelty of the research -The study offers an integrated and multidimensional framework for evaluating human capital in the digital economy.

items.title: Human Capital in AI-Enabled Digital Transformation: A Systematic Review of Workforce Competencies and HRM Mechanisms
items.abstract: This article presents a systematic literature review of the role of human capital in digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on how these developments reshape workforce competencies and human resource management (HRM) during the transition from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0. Following the PRISMA guidelines, the study combines thematic coding with comparative analysis. From an initial pool of 216 publications, 46 studies were selected for in-depth analysis. The review examines how AI and digitalisation change workforce skill requirements and how HRM mechanisms can help organisations develop and sustain the necessary competencies. The findings indicate a shift from routine and manual tasks toward hybrid competency profiles that integrate data analytics skills, AI literacy, human–machine interaction skills, and higher-order socio-cognitive capabilities, including adaptive reasoning, collaboration, and ethical judgement. HRM emerges as a strategic integrator that supports continuous reskilling, predictive skills-gap analysis, and the development of effective human–AI teams. Based on these findings, the study proposes a multilevel framework explaining how institutional mechanisms, organisational strategy, HRM practices, and human–AI complementarity jointly shape workforce competitiveness in AI-enabled digital transformation. The framework contributes to human-centric digitalisation by linking workforce competitiveness to capability velocity and human–AI complementarity. It also provides managerial implications for designing learning, governance, and decision-making structures that enable organisations to respond to evolving competency requirements and translate technological potential into sustainable operational advantages.
